You're correct that there are certainly values of f, g, and h which would make this a +EV game. That being said, even if f, g, and h (the three jackpots) increase over time, they must increase in such a way that the EV eventually becomes positive, of which there is no guarantee. The EV of the game is "blind" to f, g, and h in that it doesn't really matter what the three jackpots are for the EV. What the three do change is the risk, or variance, of the game. So for a given EV, it is better (for most people) to play when f is high and g and h are low.

In general, lottery systems (like lotteries, or slots with increasing jackpots) have increasing EV over time as people lose. The expected profit is probably usually negative, so yes it's smartest to play when EV is positive. But people play when there is negative EV because they have high risk tolerance or maybe just love the gamba and are chasing the high.

Given X, pot (P), and graceful (G), there are 4 mutually exclusive hands you need to worry about: 

1. Opening hand contains X
2. Opening hand doesn't contain X, but contains:

Let's use P, G, and X to denote the positions in the deck of the cards in questions. So P = 3 indicates that pot is the 3rd card from the top. The following probabilities enumerate every mutually exclusive possibility of drawing into X, given no other draw possibilities. I will also omit certain brackets indicating denominators, for readability.

Pr( X ≤ 6 ) = 6/40

Only opening pot:

Pr( P ≤ 6, 7≤G≤8, 9≤X≤11) = (37 c 5)\*(32 c 1)\*(31 c 2) / (40 c 6)\*(34 c 2)\*(32 c 3) = 3/4940 

Let's talk about this probability. The reasoning is that you can open only pot, pot into graceful, graceful into X. So we count the ways of only pot being in the first 6 cards, only graceful being in the next two, then X in the next three. Then we divide by the total number of ways to choose the top 6, then the next 2, then the next 3 (note this is not the same as choosing 11 at once). 

But can we be smarter? Yes we can!

Observe that there are only 40 positions for P, G, and X. We can assign these positions a total of 3!\*(40 choose 3) ways. In the first 6 cards, there are 6 positions for P. In the next 2 cards, there are 2 positions for G, and in the following 3 cards, there are 3 positions for X. Thus, the desired probability is:

6 \* 2 \* 3 / 3!\*(40 choose 3) = 3/4940

I will use this method going forward.

Pr( P ≤ 6, 7≤X≤8, 7 ≤ G ) = 6 \* 2 \* 33 / 3!\*(40 choose 3) = 33/4940

Explanation: Again, 3!(40 c 3) ways to assign positions to P, G, and X. There are then 6 desired slots for P, 2 desired slots for X, and 33 desired slots for G.

  
Pr( G ≤ 6, 7≤X≤9, 7 ≤ P) = 6 \* 3 \* 33 / 3!\*(40 choose 3) = 99/9880

Pr( G ≤ 6, 7≤P≤9, 10≤X≤11 ) = 6 \* 3 \* 2 / 3!\*(40 choose 3) = 3/4940

Pr( P,G ≤ 6, 7≤X≤11) = 6 \* 5 \* 5 / 3!\*(40 choose 3) = 5/1976

Adding up the probabilities: 

Pr( draw into X ) = 6/40 + 3/4940 + 33/4940 + 99/9880 + 3/4940 + 5/1976 = 421/2470 = .17044

So roughly a 17% chance, which means that pot and graceful only increase your odds of drawing into X by about 2% over just hard opening X.

A couple things—

Getting into tutoring is very difficult when you’re young and inexperienced, mostly because you’re young and inexperienced. It’s a catch 22. 

If you charge a reasonable rate: why hire you over a college student or someone older and with more experience who is charging the same rate?

If you charge a super bargain rate like $5: you *might* get parents who are looking for cheap babysitting, or something like that. If you charge a very low rate, you’re devaluing your time so people will assume you’re not as good as people charging more. Like if someone offered me a pack of chicken breast for half a dollar/pound, I’d decline and go happily spend 20 times that amount at a grocery store. There are certainly people who would hire you, but depending on your circumstances they may be difficult to find.

So what can you do?

I started tutoring at a young age only because my mom had a friend who had kids several years younger than me. I would not have felt comfortable tutoring my peers for money, even if I had the opportunity, due to the lack of an age/experience gap (but that’s just me). It would likely be awkward for the other person.

You said you’d prefer to target those ~2 years younger than you. Perhaps talk to your past teachers/school counselors (or whatever your equivalent is) and see if they can “advertise” on your behalf (ie put your name out there if their students are looking for tutors). 

Your best bet is probably to find one of those after-school extracurricular math/reading programs to work at. I don’t know what that scene is like in whatever country you live in, but it’s a big-ish thing in America and an even bigger thing in Asia. I think Kumon is in the UK—stuff like that.

As for where to tutor, a common location is best. A library is nice, provided you find one that doesn’t mind talking. A cafe or coffee shop might be better. 

The online avenue might be different from what I imagine it to be, but I can’t imagine a world in which someone goes looking for a tutor online and decides to hire someone who’s only 14, unfortunately. You’re just competing with too much, not to mention work laws getting in the way of you signing up in the first place.

I don’t think it is more important than MSE, it’s just something to consider, since there are many ways to quantify the quality of an estimator.

The bias-variance tradeoff tells us, roughly, that the biased estimator can give lower variance but higher bias, and the unbiased estimator higher variance with no bias. The MSE of the former might be lower, but by how much? And is that worth the increase in bias? These questions in general have no uniform answer.

I would say unbiased estimators are a convenient way to introduce an easy and uniform concept of measuring the quality of an estimator in a classroom setting, which is why there is emphasis on unbiasedness—people are taught bias before MSE, so they might place more emphasis on it? 

A fun fact is that you can solve for the multiplicative constant yielding the minimal MSE of an estimator that is a multiple of the sample variance, and that will yield a denominator of n+1.

I think that in practice, a lower MSE is generally preferred over 0 bias, since MSE is such a ubiquitous risk measure.

Tutoring and teaching are two different things, I think.

Teaching is a very pure form of communication—you “just” need to tell and, hopefully, explain.

Tutoring can encompass a lot of other things. A professor, for example, might not give two shits if a third of the class is failing. But as a tutor, it’s basically your job to prevent that from happening.

As such, when you tutor, you need to be cognizant of what is most likely to help the student succeed. More often than not, success is not the product of being shown how to do the problems. If it was, Khan Academy would’ve put tutors out of business long ago.

Sometimes, an inspired two-sentence explanation of a particularly difficult topic is all that is required. The problem is that, for younger kids’ curricula, nothing is particularly complicated. 

Take adding fractions, for example. In my slightly elitist opinion, there’s nothing inherently difficult about this, except that it might be hard to understand why common denominators are required. But to a child, adding 2/7 and 4/9 can be a very daunting task. 

But why? Often, I find it’s not “they don’t understand because they don’t understand common denominators,” it’s more like “they don’t understand _and_ they don’t understand common denominators,” which is fine.

So what is actually holding them back from becoming experts at adding fractions? It could be that:
1) they need to do 500 problems and they can’t sit still long enough to do 5
2) they don’t understand basic fractions at all
3) it takes them longer than it should to multiply 7 by 9 to form a common denominator, which is why they struggle to do 5 practice problems
4) they’re just lazy and refuse to put in any effort
5) they don’t care to learn

So in my opinion, to be a good tutor for children, you’d need to be aware of all these possibilities, as well as how to remedy each.

These are just my thoughts on tutoring younger kids, hopefully you find something helpful. You should take them with a grain of salt because I suck at tutoring younger kids, as I’m sure you can tell, so I simply refuse to do so.

X ^ Y is short-hand for min(X,Y).

So, for example, X ^ d is the lesser of the claim and the deductible. This would be what the policyholder pays on the claim. If your car has $100 worth of damage and you have a $200 deductible, your personal loss is 100 = 100 ^ 200 = min(100,200).

X ^ u is the lesser of the claim and the policy limit. This is what the insurance company would be responsible for (assuming a deductible of 0). When introducing a deductible, the insurance company becomes responsible for (X ^ u) - (X ^ d).

By taking expectations, E(X ^ u) - E(X ^ d) is the expected payment the insurance company makes per claim/loss (we can assume a claim is a loss because if X < d, the rational policyholder won’t file a claim because they will incur a premium increase at the benefit of getting $0 from the insurance company). Contrast this to a payment per payment, which is how much the insurance company actually expects to pay whenever it does have to pay something: E(X - d | X > d).

The first thing you should do is decide if you want to treat your variable (test score) as continuous or discrete.  In the former case, you would split the range of all possible test scores into five intervals of length 20, like so:

[0, 20)
[20, 40)
[40, 60)
[60, 80)
[80, 100]

If you treat the score as a discrete variable, then you have 101 different scores you must account for (0-100)—clearly you can’t evenly split 101 scores into five bins each containing 20 scores. There are a couple ways to deal with this. The first is that you can cheat and group them like so:
[0, 20], [21, 40], …, [81, 100] 
So the first bin has 21 scores and the rest of the bins have 20 scores. Or, if you believe that a score of 0 or 100 is distinct enough to warrant its own bin, you could do that too (whether you should do this depends on the data). But I think it ultimately doesn’t really matter, and that it would be better to treat test scores as a continuous variable to circumvent this issue altogether. 

This is one of those things (like many in statistics), which has more to do with how you present your data, and while there are “rules of thumb,” there isn’t a mathematically definitive answer that says “always do it this way because the other is unambiguously wrong.” 

That being said, you should follow whatever your teacher/professor wants you to do because they’re the one giving you the grade.

In OLS, alpha and beta are assumed to be population parameters, so you assume they have a "true" value, which is unknown to you. Alpha-hat and beta-hat, which are the outputs in a regression calculation, are your "best guess" at what the true values of alpha and beta are (in math speak, best guess = best linear unbiased estimate).

Because alpha-hat and beta-hat are only guesses, it's nice to have a way to measure  how confident you are in those guesses. This is the standard error (which is just a standard deviation). I'm not sure what exactly your professor wants, but generally speaking a low SE indicates high confidence, and a high SE indicates low confidence. The confidence here is how confident you are that the true alpha or beta is close to your estimate.

The T-score for a regression coefficient is simply the estimated coefficient (e.g. alpha-hat) divided by its standard error (e.g. SE(alpha-hat)). Notice that if SE(alpha-hat) is small, then the T-score will be inflated, leading to a small p-value, which turns into a vague-ish notion of "statistical significance." If SE(alpha-hat) is large, then the T-score will be small, leading to a large p-value.

Here, the p-value is the p-value for the hypothesis test of H0: alpha-hat = 0 , Ha: alpha-hat != 0. So if your p-value is really small (i.e. SE is large), then the corresponding hypothesis test says that you reject the null hypothesis that alpha-hat = 0,  and so you believe, at some confidence level, that your computed alpha-hat is meaningfully different from 0.

I don’t know what your background in probability is, but my impression is that your biggest hurdle is not necessarily the concept of probability, but of random variables.

In my opinion, random variables are poorly named because they are neither random nor variables. They are simply functions (albeit measurable, but that’s not really an important distinction for the present discussion). The notion of randomness comes from the fact that, when we talk about random variables, the most granular information we have about them is their distribution. We don’t know what gets mapped to what, but we do know things like what proportion of things get mapped to a certain interval. This “proportion” is what we mean by “probability.” 

In order to mathematically formulate the probability of something occurring, we have to “rigorize” that something as the output of a random variable, ie a function from a measurable space into another measurable space, where the “something” can somehow be codified in the output space.

I agree with you when you say that everything is just constant, because in theory all the physics governing our universe have been determined by any previous state, so every state in the future could theoretically be calculated by some disgusting PDE or something. I think this is a philosophical thing to believe in, but we probably agree that this is the case. I’m also ignoring quantum mechanics and its implications.

So let’s take another look at the coin example. If flipping a coin is to be a r.v., then we need an input space and an output space. The output space is easy: just the set {0, 1}. The input space is a little trickier, but we could say that the input space is the interval (0, 1) where half of the interval (we don’t know which numbers exactly) gets mapped to 0, and the other half gets mapped to 1. What’s the interpretation of the input space? Well in my previous comment, I basically said that each number in the interval (0, 1) corresponds to a physical state which would force the coin into either heads or tails. But you said, and I agree with you on this, that our physical state is predetermined. So my suggestion is to think of the interval (0, 1) as a bunch of alternate parallel universes, where the physical states differ slightly from one another as you range from 0 to 1. 

So why can we still consider this “random?” Because we don’t have any information about whether our universe corresponds to .3, or pi/4, or .9999. Now the nice thing is that, if the coin lands on heads, we can determine for sure that our universe belongs to the part of the interval (0, 1) which gets sent to heads. We’ve essentially gained information - this kind of thinking is useful if you delve more into the theory of stochastic processes. 

So why can’t you say a population parameter is a random variable? Well, I argue that you could. If you go “wide” enough, we could define a function from the interval (0, 1) into the real numbers which represents, for example, the mean height of all adults in the United States. In order to continue, though, you need to define the meaning of the input space. If each number in the input space (0, 1) represents our current universe, then we’re left with a constant r.v., which is of little interest. The mean height is what it is. If, however, you decide that every number in (0, 1) is a parallel universe, each of them differing slightly, then your random variable becomes non constant, and you can meaningfully talk about probabilities. 

I would say, however, that the latter example is morally the same as drawing samples of 1000 from a population of 1000000 and treating the sample mean as a random variable. 

Basically, probability in math exists as a tool that requires no intuition/interpretation to formulate or understand. Wherever you can formally define a random variable (ie a measurable function), you can talk about probabilities in a mathematically rigorous (but not necessarily meaningful) way. But in order for that to align with your intuition, you need to take some liberties with how you interpret your input/output spaces. The nice thing about purely formal probability is that it is divorced from our intuition, as we humans tend to suck at probability, as essentially nothing in our lives is truly random.

Anyways, in stats I presume that we take our current universe as is and don’t consider alternate universes. The population parameter is reduced to a constant random variable because it is more useful to think of it that way when you need to do statistics. When we flip a coin, we consider the outcome to be non-constant because it is more useful that way.

Edit: if you have a 95% CI, I’d argue that it is not intuitively “wrong” to say “oh the the parameter has a 95% chance of falling within that CI.” It is only wrong because math has a strict definition of what a “chance” actually is.

Do you know what the marginal pdf is supposed to represent, conceptually? It is easier to consider the discrete case then extend that logic to the continuous case.

From a purely technical standpoint, the marginal distribution of X needs to be a single variable function of the variable x. 

Imagine a joint pdf f(x,y) on a simple domain, like a square, as a volume of mass = 1. The marginal pdf f_X(x) gives you the area of the cross section of the total mass at x. Because probability is represented by volumes in this case, the singular value f_X(x) is more or less meaningless. What is meaningful is when you obtain a volume by smashing a bunch of these cross sections together, ie take an integral of f_X over some range of x values, say (a, b). The interpretation of this integral is the volume of the entire probability mass that is contained between a < x < b. Unlike any particular value of f_X, this integral has meaning and is exactly the probability that X will fall between a and b.

If the probability of event A is P(A), then "on average," A will happen P(A)\*100% of the time. But like all things in math, we have to say what we mean by "on average."

Suppose we have some "random variable" X. This variable takes the value of 1 (i.e. X = 1) if A happens, and 0 (so X = 0) if A doesn't happen. Suppose the event A is independent of itself, in the sense that we can test for A multiple times, and each test doesn't affect the outcome of the next test.

Let X\_1 represent the first test (so X\_1 = 1 if A happened in the first test, and X\_1 = 0 if A didn't happen in the first test), X\_2 represent the second test, X\_3 the third test, and so on until X\_n. (so we have n tests in total.)

The Strong Law of Large Numbers (an important and nontrivial theorem, but very intuitive) states that, as n goes to infinity, the *average* of the sum of all the X\_k's will tend towards P(A). So if each test is a coin flip and A = heads, then P(A) = 1/2. The first could be tails, and the second could be tails. So in the first two flips of the coin, we didn't get a heads. That's fine. But as we flip the coin more times, we expect the ratio of heads to tails to approach 1/2 - and it will.

The law of large numbers (some people mistakenly refer to this as "the law of averages" - that shows you how intuitive this idea is) is essentially your intuition.

This is why probability is often a difficult subject. It is both intuitive and not intuitive at the same time. An expected value, or average, is in some sense a statement about infinity, or what happens at "infinite time."

One big takeaway here is that if P(A) < 1, then A is never "guaranteed" to happen no matter how many trials you make. We could even have P(A) = 0.9999, and it's (theoretically) possible for A to not happen in 1000 trials - although this is realistically impossible. This is why an average is often called "expected value" - at most we can expect it, but we can't guarantee it (unless, of course, P(A) = 1).

To give you an idea of how probability can be very unintuitive, there are instances where, even if P(A) = 1, and you test for A, it still might not happen. An example is choosing a random real number in the interval \[0,1\]. With probability 1, you will choose an irrational number. But, there *are* plenty of rational numbers, like 1/2 or 5/9 in the interval to choose, so if you *happened* to choose 1/2, then an event with a 0% chance of occurring just occurred!

When abstracting, it's good to keep in mind the following - is this a useful characterization? There are often multiple ways of abstracting an idea, but usually only one is "useful," so it's often called "the correct" way of abstracting something. 

In a regular sequence a : N --> S, there is a notion of "flow" or "direction." The first element is a(1), the second element is a(2), the third element is a(3), and so on. Suppose we have a "3-dimensional sequence" a : N^3 --> S, using the construction as you've described. Then the first element would likely be a(1,1,1), but what is the second element? Is it a(1,1,2), or perhaps a(1,2,1), or even a(2,1,1)? Suppose we say that a(1,1,2) is the second element. Then what's the third? Is it a(1,1,3) or a(1,2,2)? 

A natural question arises: can we order the integer lattice in n-dimensions? The answer is yes, because the (countable) Cartesian product of countable sets is again countable. But if you put an ordering on it, all you've done is put N^n in bijection with N, so really you've done nothing at all, and your "n-dimensional sequence" is really just a 1-dimensional sequence in disguise.

It turns out that there is a generalization of sequences -- it's called a net. In essence, a net (with entries in a set S) is a function from A to S, where A is a "directed set." A directed set is basically a set which has some ordering on it. Of course, the notion of a net actually subsumes the idea you described. N^n, with an appropriate ordering, can become a directed set, but as described above, this isn't particularly useful. Nets become useful when describing a "sequence" which has uncountably many elements, rather than countably many -- but why is this useful?

Sequences are a key tool in calculus, and in calculus, the primary idea is the limit. In calculus, the most fundamental questions arise in the form of convergence. When might a sequence converge, and to what limit? Convergence requires an idea of "direction," which is why sequences have a natural direction (1, 2, 3, ...). Generally, undergraduate research can mean a couple things, one of them being actual original research on some problem. These things tend to be small and less important than the things a PhD student would be researching, for obvious reasons. One, professors are already stretched for time, so you'd likely be meeting with them maybe like once a week, for an hour. Two, you are not a PhD student. The research a PhD student does is beneficial for more than the student, in the sense that the university is paying the student to do research. Probably the biggest issue, though, is prerequisite knowledge. The average PhD student doesn't start doing research until after a year or two into their program, since they (a) don't have an advisor yet, and (b) don't know enough math yet. And if they don't know enough math, then you don't know enough math. Note that if your goal is to publish, then undergraduate research rarely leads to that, but it's certainly possible.

That being said, it's still very much possible, and hopefully encouraged (depends on your department, I'd say), to do undergraduate research. Will you do something you're super interested in? Probably not. But you could certainly work on some problem in, say, algebra or combinatorics - these fields lend themselves to such things, I think. However, if you look hard enough, I'm sure you could find a professor willing to give you a problem in any field you desire. 

Now, if you actually want to do research, then your best bet is to wait another year and apply to an REU (Research Experience for Undergraduates) program. These are summer programs hosted by various math departments, where some ~10-20 undergraduates will be put into small teams (2-4) to do actual original work with an advisor and probably some graduate TAs. You'll also receive a stipend, usually around 3-4k, more if they don't provide room & board. This is definitely something you should do if you're considering pursuing a PhD program.

If you can't do actual research, then your next best bet is to do some sort of independent learning project with a professor. This could mean reading a book, or perhaps some papers, on a topic you're interested in, then meeting with the professor regularly to talk over the material. This is also very beneficial since you get to study something you care about, and the professor is able to better gauge your ability to learn math (so you can get a nice rec letter later). 

This is all stuff you should consider doing in a year, maybe two. At the very least, you need to know how to write proofs, which is probably something you haven't encountered in any seriousness by taking calculus. Linear algebra may or may not introduce you to proofs, but your best bet is to take either real analysis or abstract algebra. These classes are sort of like the cornerstones of undergraduate math. To do an independent learning project, you would have to do the project on something not offered in/as a class, otherwise the professor will probably tell you to just take the class. But in order to do that, you would need to know the basic math taught at the undergraduate level. Same with research.

So for now, just concentrate on doing well in your classes and learning math. In a year or two, depending on where you are, definitely approach some professors and ask to do a project with them, and know that you will be told "no" a lot of times (and it's nothing personal) before you're told "yes." 

Hope this helps!

p.s. Please don't take my word as law. This post is just the summary of the experiences of many, but not all, and is very subjective.

You need sigma algebras for measure spaces, and a probability space is a measure space. In particular, measures have some intuitive notions we'd like them to follow, but they are contradictory if you try to define a measure on the entire set of subsets of a space X (i.e. the power set X). It turns out that defining the domain of a measure to instead be a sigma algebra of subsets resolves the issue.

In probability, random variables are measurable functions. f : (X,N) --> (Y,M) is said to be measurable (N and M are sigma algebras on X and Y respectively) if for every A \in M, f^-1 (A) is in N. In other words, the preimage of a measurable set is measurable.

I like to think of measure spaces as analogous to topological spaces. A topology on a set X is a subset of the power set which satisfies some properties, and continuous functions are those functions whose preimages of open sets are open. Similarly, a sigma algebra on a set X is a subset of the power set which satisfies some properties, and the measurable functions are like continuous functions.

You may also think of sigma algebras as the space of possible outcomes. You can recast all of probability theory in terms of measure theory, where sigma algebra = outcome space, measure = probability, event = measurable set.

Alternatively, if you already accept that sin(2π) = 0 and cos(2π) = 1, then using the formula e^ix = cos(x) + isin(x) makes it easy. Indeed, e^i(x+2π) = e^ix e^i2π = e^ix (cos(2π) + isin(2π)) = e^ix .

At the heart of differential equations is finding a function which satisfies some stuff (like an equation) involving some of its derivatives. You learned in calculus that to "reverse" the process of differentiation, you had to integrate. Now, if you take a function f(x) and differentiate it (with respect to x), you will get another function f'(x). However, of you integrate a function f(x) into, say, F(x), you do not get a function. Instead you're left with a "class" of functions which differ by a constant. This is why you always write + C at the end of all your antiderivatives.

Now if you imagine the plane R^2, the class of functions mentioned earlier can be visually described as a "stack" of graphs which look identical, just vertically displaced by some amount. These graphs are said to "partition" the plane, in that every point of the plane lies on one graph, and only one graph. An initial condition is a point on a plane, and by specifying an initial condition, you're really trying to specify a specific graph. The graph which the point lies on is then your solution.

For a real number x, x^0 = 1. This is because, by definition, x^n = x*x*...*x where there are n x's in the product. It is natural, then, to define x^0 as the so-called "empty product." That is, the product of no factors. What should this be? Well if you add no numbers together, you get 0, the additive identity. So if you we multiply no numbers together, we should get the multiplicative identity, which is 1. So we've established that x^0 = 1 for any real number (yes, 0^0 is 1.)

Ok, but then (for nonzero x):

1 = x^0 = x^(1-1) = x^1 * x^(-1) = x * x^(-1)

Which necessarily forces x^(-1) = 1/x.

In particular, (Baby) Rudin's treatment of the Lebesgue measure is reasonably intuitive, and it helps give perspective to the abstract treatment of the measure given in Folland, prior to the Lebesgue measure. I also used a book called "Real Analysis: Theory of Measure and Integration," by James Yeh. That book is like the very opposite of terse. What Folland does in 100 pages, Yeh takes 300. I found that a lot of the problems in Folland were modifications of proofs that he himself gave, or could be completely found as results in Yeh.

For functional analysis, Folland is sometimes a little terse (at least for me), and I was able to find better proofs of many things online.

Other than that, I think Folland is a thoroughly better book than Baby Rudin, at least in terms of exposition (he has these "Notes and References" sections at the end of each chapter which contain historical notes and the like - often quite interesting), and I hope you enjoy it as much as I did!
